dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is five days old, and it's a cold, damp Friday to stay in with him. Overnight, Iran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar tied to seven demands, while tankers keep getting hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and chip stocks are bouncing this morning after Thursday's 5.52% Nasdaq drop into correction. Solon tops out near 49° with temperatures falling through the day and showers likely by evening, so any errands are better done early. Tonight is a sports doubleheader from the couch: Ohio State hoops opens at home against Youngstown State at 6:30 PM, and the Cavs host the 8-1 76ers at 7:30 PM in an NBA Cup game, with Jarrett Allen questionable. Locally, the Ohio Hazmat Teams Conference runs today and tomorrow at the Solon Community Center.

weekBrief.text: Benji's first week wraps up as a quiet, stay-home stretch — born Sunday, home Tuesday, pediatrician Wednesday, and now five days old with the house settling into a rhythm around him. Solon's weather turns cold and damp for the weekend — 49° with evening showers Friday and 46° Saturday — then breaks sunny and warmer Sunday at 57°, peaking near 61° Tuesday before cooling again. The sports weekend is stacked: the Cavs host Philadelphia tonight and the Knicks Saturday, Ohio State football hosts Oregon Saturday afternoon, and the Browns visit the Saints Sunday with Shedeur Sanders in line for his first start of the season. The week's standout grocery move stays the Thanksgiving stock-up — Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb — and if energy allows, Hadestown continues at Playhouse Square this weekend.

Trump says he will decide 'soon' whether to resume the war in Iran
items.summary:
President Trump told reporters on Thursday that he will decide soon whether the United States resumes major military action against Iran, after meeting his national security advisers for the first time since the midterm elections. He said he would rather not destroy what remains of the country, but added that he may have to, and promised the answer would come soon.

Reporting based on U.S. officials describes three paths on the table: a new round of airstrikes aimed at Iran's nuclear program, continued economic pressure through sanctions and the blockade of Iranian ports, or a negotiated deal involving significant concessions. U.S. Central Command is said to be finalizing preparations for a possible return to major combat, though it has not received any new order.

The decision lands just days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in an election where the war was a central issue. Mediators in Qatar are circulating a short confidence-building draft as an off-ramp, which makes the next few days a genuine fork between escalation and diplomacy.

Watch for any formal statement from the White House, and for movement on the Qatari draft, which would be the first sign the deal path is winning.

items.title: Iran's nuclear proposal reaches Washington through Qatar — with seven conditions attached
items.summary:
Iran has passed a proposal on its nuclear program to the United States through Qatari mediators, according to a senior Iranian official who spoke to Reuters. Tehran says the document comes with seven conditions that must be met before it will negotiate in earnest or reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Three of the demands have been named publicly: lifting U.S. sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, and paying war reparations. A separate draft described by Qatari intermediaries would have international inspectors invited back to bombed nuclear sites and the strait reopened before full nuclear talks resume, though it is not clear whether that is the same document Washington is reviewing.

Iranian officials spent Thursday working the phones and the map — the foreign minister spoke with regional counterparts including Qatar's, while a senior security official was in Moscow meeting President Putin. Meanwhile, tanker traffic through Hormuz remains dangerous, with more vessels reported damaged this week after the worst month of attacks yet in October.

Both sides say they are still far apart, so this is best read as an opening bid. The next signal is whether Washington responds to the conditions publicly or quietly keeps the Qatar channel moving.

items.title: A third U.S. aircraft carrier will not reach the Middle East before mid-November
items.summary:
The USS Theodore Roosevelt will not arrive in the Middle East before mid-November, according to Axios reporting citing a U.S. official. The carrier is due to begin a port call in Singapore on Friday that will last several days, which pushes its timeline back.

When it does arrive, the Roosevelt would be the third American carrier in the region, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington. It is still unclear whether it is meant to relieve one of them or to add to the force already on station. Its strike group, together with a Marine expeditionary unit, represents roughly 10,000 personnel.

The timing matters because it overlaps with President Trump's pending decision on whether to resume strikes on Iran. Tehran has said it would widen its retaliation if the war restarts, and mediators have been stepping up efforts to head that off.

The carrier left San Diego in late September. Watch for its departure from Singapore, which will set the real arrival window.

items.title: Zelenskiy says Ukraine must adapt to the new politics in Washington — and fix its Patriot shortage
items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy says Kyiv has to adjust to the changed political landscape in the United States after the midterms, and build a working dialogue to keep aid and air defenses flowing. He made the comments in an interview broadcast Thursday while attending a summit in Spain.

His most urgent problem, he said, is Patriot air defense missiles, calling it the number one priority and warning things get very tough for Ukraine without a solution. He also says Ukraine is still owed about $16 billion in assistance that Washington promised but did not deliver, and is working to keep enough F-16s flying over the next several months.

The backdrop is awkward: the State Department recently approved a sale of 500 Patriot missiles worth about $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected until the early 2030s — far too late for the current war. U.S.-led talks involving Ukraine and Russia are scheduled to resume next week in Abu Dhabi.

What to watch is whether the new Congress moves any faster on Ukraine aid than the outgoing one, and whether the Abu Dhabi round produces anything concrete.

items.title: Israel's president says Trump's move to end U.S. aid landed 'like a bolt from the blue'
items.summary:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog says President Trump's announcement this week that he would end U.S. aid to Israel came as a complete shock, describing it as like a bolt from the blue. He raised the issue in a meeting with the Yashar party, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

Israel is in the middle of a government-formation fight at the same time. After last month's election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 of 120 Knesset seats, short of a majority, and in consultations with Herzog he secured only 46 endorsements after an ultra-Orthodox ally declined to back him. Eisenkot, by contrast, has lined up support from 67 seats, though 19 of them come from Arab-led parties, which complicates his path.

Herzog says he will decide on Sunday who gets the first mandate to try to form a government; that person then has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister in the meantime and is challenging the election results, claiming the vote was stolen.

Between the aid cutoff and the coalition math, Israel faces its most uncertain political stretch in years. Sunday's mandate decision is the next milestone.

items.title: Vance privately blasts Netanyahu as the Iran war splits the Trump administration
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance has privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being wrong on everything about the Iran war, according to reporting sourced to people familiar with his comments. Publicly, Vance has been just as blunt about the politics, posting that the reason Republicans lost the midterms is the war.

The split inside the administration is now well documented: Vance has led the faction urging a negotiated settlement, and last month sent a letter through Qatari intermediaries proposing renewed peace talks — an outreach the president backed. On the other side, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Netanyahu have favored resuming strikes, which Trump held off doing before the election.

This is also early positioning for 2028. Vance, Senator Ted Cruz, and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis are already offering competing explanations for the Republican defeat, and the Iran argument is becoming the first real fault line of that race.

Watch whether Vance's public campaign for a deal survives the president's pending decision on resuming strikes — that call will show whose advice carried the day.

items.title: Trump heads to Florida in his first trip since the midterm rout
items.summary:
President Trump travels to Florida on Friday, his first trip outside Washington since Democrats swept the midterms. He is scheduled to speak in the late afternoon at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral before continuing on to Palm Beach.

The trip follows an unusually quiet few days for the president, whose only public appearances since the election have centered on White House renovations. It also comes days after he signed a proclamation declaring that outer space beyond Earth is open to exploration by all — a fitting backdrop for a speech at the space center.

The scale of Tuesday's loss is still sinking in: Democrats flipped 39 House seats and seven Senate seats, winning districts Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and even flipping ground in red states like Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas. Fresh exit polling suggests Black voter support for Democrats approached levels last seen in Barack Obama's 2008 campaign.

Friday's remarks are the first real chance to hear how Trump intends to govern with a Democratic Congress — and how he plans to handle an already-forming Republican blame game over the defeat.

items.title: Two Senate races are still uncalled — Alaska and Mississippi will set the size of the Democratic majority
items.summary:
Democrats will enter January with at least 54 Senate seats, but two races remained too close to call on Friday morning, and winning both would push their majority to 56. More than 25 House races are also still undecided.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by roughly 1,800 to 2,100 votes with about 95 percent counted. Thousands of mail and affidavit ballots are still outstanding; mail ballots can arrive within five business days, and counties must certify by November 13. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Dan Sullivan by only about 600 votes with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted.

Alaska has an extra wrinkle: its ranked-choice system means that if no candidate clears 50 percent on first choices, a tabulation round is scheduled for November 18, and counting is slowed further by the state's geography. The race was also roiled by a second, unrelated Dan Sullivan appearing on the ballot, prompting Trump to demand the other Sullivan's votes be given to the senator.

Neither race changes who controls the Senate, but the margin matters for filibuster strategy and oversight leverage. Expect Mississippi to resolve first.

items.title: Schumer vows Senate Democrats will block any Trump 'right-winger' on the Supreme Court
items.summary:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer told the Associated Press on Thursday that his party will not allow President Trump to place a right-winger on the Supreme Court once Democrats take control of the chamber. He extended the pledge to lower-court and Cabinet nominees he described in blunter terms.

Pressed on whether Democrats would hold a vacancy open until after the next presidential election — the playbook Mitch McConnell used in 2016 — Schumer would not commit either way. For now the fight is theoretical: there is no vacancy, and the court's two oldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, have both said they do not intend to retire.

The comments came two days after Democrats won a decisive Senate majority, which Schumer argues could reach 56 seats depending on the two uncalled races. The new Congress does not convene until January; Republicans hold the Senate until then. Schumer says the Democratic agenda will focus on costs — health care, housing, tariffs, child care, and energy.

The vow sets up a guaranteed collision if any justice does step down in the next two years.

items.title: Justice Department civil rights chief Harmeet Dhillon resigns — the first senior exit since the midterms
items.summary:
Harmeet Dhillon, who has led the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division since April 2025, resigned on Thursday. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced the departure and praised her leadership, making her the first senior Justice Department official to leave since the Republican midterm losses.

Dhillon says the decision was hers: she described the job as grueling, noted she had lost her husband and her father before the 2024 election, and said she told the White House back in October that she planned to return to private practice at her law firm. Reports linking the exit to a television appearance have been denied.

Her tenure remade the division. Roughly three-quarters of its lawyers — about 300 of 400 — left during her first seven months, and its focus shifted toward anti-DEI investigations, religious liberty, gun rights, election integrity, and cases involving transgender policies in schools and university admissions.

No successor or final day has been named. Incoming Democratic committee control in Congress is likely to bring new scrutiny of the department, which may shape who is willing to take the job next.

items.title: Massie plans to force a House vote next week on impeaching Defense Secretary Hegseth
items.summary:
Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky intends to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as early as the week of November 9, when the House returns. His spokesperson confirmed the plan this week, and Massie has said the only thing that would stop him is Hegseth resigning.

The resolution carries eight articles of impeachment, first introduced in September in a 34-page document accusing Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution during the Iran war, among other charges. That earlier effort stalled when Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House into a seven-week recess and dismissed the move as a stunt.

Because the resolution is privileged, if the parliamentarian affirms it, the Speaker has up to two legislative days to schedule a vote or a motion to table it. Impeachment would take a simple House majority; removal would then require two-thirds of the Senate, which remains unlikely. Massie, who lost his primary and is serving out a lame-duck session, puts his own odds of passing the House at better than 50 percent, and some Republican sources agree it could pass.

Hegseth posted a video Thursday vowing to continue, and Trump praised him the same day, saying no Cabinet changes are planned. Next week's floor fight will test both statements.

items.title: California's governor commutes every death sentence in the state — all 548 of them
items.summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he is commuting the death sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life in prison without parole. The group — 529 men and 19 women — makes up more than a quarter of everyone on death row in the United States.

It is described by the Death Penalty Information Center as the largest mass commutation in American history. California has not carried out an execution since 2006, and Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019. In an open letter he called the death penalty unjust, error-prone, and incompatible with the state's values. Forty-five of the 548 had exhausted their appeals.

The legal path is split: 166 commutations can take effect immediately, but 382 cases involve multiple felony convictions and need the California Supreme Court's approval, requiring at least four of seven justices. Newsom has asked the court to return its recommendations by the end of 2026, before his term ends in January. The death penalty itself remains legal in California — prosecutors can still seek it in future cases.

Reaction split fast on Friday, with Riverside County's district attorney and sheriff blasting the decision and saying prosecutors and victims' families were not notified beforehand.

items.title: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks claw back part of Thursday's historic selloff
items.summary:
The Nasdaq climbed back on Friday morning as chipmakers recovered from one of the worst technology selloffs in years. By mid-morning the index was up about 1.7 percent and the S&P 500 about 1 percent, while the Dow hovered near flat — a partial repair job, not a full reversal.

Thursday's damage set the scale: the Nasdaq fell 5.52 percent, its steepest one-day drop in 19 months, confirming a correction, and the semiconductor index plunged more than 12 percent. On Friday that same chip index rose about 4.6 percent, with Nvidia up roughly 5.6 percent after losing 9 percent the day before, and AMD, Intel, and Micron posting gains in the mid-single digits to low double digits.

Traders blamed Thursday's rout on fears that a Democratic-led Congress could tighten regulation of AI and data centers, and Friday's bounce was capped by the strong jobs report, which raised expectations the Federal Reserve might hike rates in December. Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX, eased after its biggest one-day jump in about 19 months.

Whether this is a genuine bottom or a one-day breather likely depends on next week's inflation data and on whether the Anthropic roadshow steadies AI sentiment.

items.title: October hiring crushes expectations: 165,000 jobs added, unemployment down to 4.1 percent
items.summary:
The Labor Department reported Friday that employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than double the roughly 65,000 economists had forecast. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent from 4.2 percent, and the report was stronger after revisions, too — September was revised up to 60,000 and August to 186,000, adding 84,000 jobs to the record.

Professional and business services did the heavy lifting with 70,000 new jobs, followed by health care at 42,000, transportation and warehousing at 25,000, and manufacturing at 19,000. Pay rose 14 cents an hour, or 0.4 percent, to an average of $38.00 — up 3.1 percent over the year, still a touch behind the most recent inflation reading of 3.7 percent.

For markets, the good news came with a catch: traders raised the odds of a December Federal Reserve rate hike to about 78 percent, and Treasury yields moved higher. A labor market this firm gives the Fed little reason to ease.

The next big test is Tuesday's October inflation report, the last major data point before the Fed's final meeting of the year.

items.title: AI backlash reaches the IPO market: investors are pushing back on Anthropic's price tag
items.summary:
Anthropic's plan to take its AI business public is running into the same skepticism that just knocked trillions off tech stocks. Potential investors are questioning whether the company can hold its planned roadshow next week for a November listing, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The argument is about price. A valuation around $1.5 trillion has been discussed as the high end, but at least three major investors say it likely needs to come down — one suggested something closer to $1 trillion — and the raise may land nearer $80 billion than the anticipated $100 billion. Investors are also waiting on an October revenue figure that was left blank in the company's updated filing, though reporting puts its revenue run rate above $80 billion at the end of October.

Anthropic publicly filed its S-1 in late October and amended it this week, with the ticker ANT planned. The company, which has a record of quarterly losses and enormous AI buildout commitments, declined to comment.

If the roadshow slips or the price drops materially, it will be read as the clearest sign yet that the AI trade's easy money phase is over.

items.title: Airbnb and Cloudflare buck the rout with big earnings beats
items.summary:
Two companies managed to swim against this week's market current. Airbnb rose about 9 percent on Friday after a third-quarter double beat — earnings of $3.16 a share against $2.85 expected, revenue up 19 percent to $4.87 billion, and net income of $1.89 billion.

Airbnb also raised its full-year outlook to high-teens revenue growth, guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $3.22 and $3.28 billion, and authorized an additional $12 billion in share buybacks on top of the $2.7 billion it still had available. Cloudflare had a similar day, advancing about 11 percent after revenue grew 39 percent to $782.5 million, beating earnings estimates, with free cash flow of $82.1 million.

Cloudflare lifted its full-year revenue guidance to just under $3 billion and guided the fourth quarter to about $845 million. Both stocks had been knocked down in Thursday's selloff — Cloudflare fell 8 percent that day — which made Friday's rebounds sharper.

In a week defined by AI anxiety, two profitable, growing, cash-generating tech names were exactly what nervous investors wanted to buy.

items.title: Moderna posts a surprise profit — its first profitable quarter in two years
items.summary:
Moderna gave investors a genuine surprise on Friday morning, reporting third-quarter results that blew past expectations. Revenue came in at $1.31 billion, up 29 percent from a year earlier and far above the roughly $885 million analysts had penciled in.

The bottom line flipped, too: net income of $162 million, or 38 cents a share, against a loss a year ago and an expected loss of more than a dollar a share. U.S. sales accounted for $780 million and international sales $533 million, with overseas COVID vaccine sales a particular strength alongside government contracts in the U.K., Canada, and Australia. Research spending fell 27 percent as late-stage studies wrapped up and cost cuts bit.

Management raised the outlook along with the results, lifting full-year revenue growth guidance to 15 to 25 percent and the year-end cash forecast to between $8.1 and $8.3 billion — up from a previous range near $5 billion. Shares jumped about 10 percent in premarket trading.

For a company written off by many after the pandemic boom faded, a profitable quarter plus a much bigger cash cushion buys real time to prove its pipeline.

items.title: Axon bets another $1.2 billion on drone maker Skydio — and trims its own outlook
items.summary:
Axon, the company behind Tasers and police body cameras, announced Thursday it is investing another $1.2 billion in drone maker Skydio, lifting its stake to about 37 percent at a $5.2 billion pre-money valuation. The deal, a mix of cash and stock, is expected to close around the turn of the year.

The investment makes Axon the exclusive distributor of Skydio drones to U.S. and Canadian public-safety agencies, tightening the link between Axon's camera and records ecosystem and the drones increasingly used as first responders. Axon's own third quarter was a record: revenue of $909 million, up 28 percent from a year earlier.

The catch came in the guidance. Axon trimmed its full-year 2026 growth forecast to about 30 percent from a range of 32 to 34 percent, citing the exclusion of three federal Dedrone deployments worth roughly $130 million. Investors focused on that, sending the shares down about 10 percent on Friday.

The story captures the week in miniature: strong underlying demand for public-safety and defense technology, punished anyway in a market in no mood for trimmed forecasts.

items.title: Progressive council member Nithya Raman ousts Mayor Karen Bass in Los Angeles
items.summary:
Los Angeles has voted out its mayor. City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass by roughly four percentage points, according to county results and multiple projections, becoming the first challenger to unseat a sitting Los Angeles mayor since 2005.

Bass, the city's first woman mayor, elected in 2022, conceded and called Raman to congratulate her on Thursday. Raman, 45, is an urban planner trained at MIT and Harvard and a member endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, who ran to Bass's left on housing and homelessness. The count stood at about 52 percent to 48 percent.

County officials are scheduled to certify the results on November 27, and Raman's four-year term begins December 14. She inherits a homelessness crisis, a depleted police force, punishing housing costs, and the small matter of preparing the city for the 2028 Olympics.

The result is the latest sign of a restless national electorate in this cycle — incumbents who looked safe a year ago have been losing across the map.

items.title: A judge blocks Trump's triumphal arch within an hour of the panel that approved it
items.summary:
The fight over President Trump's planned 250-foot triumphal arch escalated quickly on Thursday. The National Capital Planning Commission voted 8 to 4 to approve the monument — and within about an hour, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan blocked any work from starting for 14 days.

The arch, modeled on the Arc de Triomphe, would rise at Memorial Circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, towering over the Lincoln Memorial itself. The lawsuit was brought by three Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian, joined by the attorneys general of Washington, D.C., and Virginia, who argue the project needs congressional approval and would harm the environment, traffic, and the historic viewshed.

The judge's order, which covers excavation, road closures, and other construction-related work, cited the plaintiffs' likelihood of success on the congressional-approval question. Commissioners backing the project framed it as a marker for the nation's 250th anniversary.

Fourteen days is a pause, not a verdict — but the legal theory behind the block, that Congress never authorized this, is the one the whole project will ultimately stand or fall on.

items.title: Revealed: the U.S. held talks with Iran about deportations — in the middle of the war
items.summary:
Court documents unsealed on Thursday show the Trump administration held talks with Iran about deporting Iranian nationals even as the two countries were at war, the Associated Press reports. The contacts concerned travel documents and possible routes for removals.

As recently as mid-October, the government told a court it planned to carry out deportations through an unnamed third country. The legal group behind the lawsuit says at least a dozen ICE detainees were told in the past week they could be deported to Iran, some as soon as this Sunday, routed through Pakistan. The suit also alleges immigration agencies shared confidential asylum-seeker information with Iran, which the Department of Homeland Security denies.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has ordered the government to give the court 24 hours' notice of any finalized deportation plan and five days' written notice before any removal. At an October hearing she warned that returnees would face, at minimum, a serious threat of certain death, and threatened contempt if her order were violated.

The disclosure underscores how many channels between Washington and Tehran stayed open beneath the fighting — and sets up a courtroom confrontation if any flight is scheduled.

items.title: No, California's election-night governor call was not proof of rigging, Reuters fact-check finds
items.summary:
A claim spreading online — that the Associated Press calling California's governor's race at the moment polls closed proves the election was rigged — does not hold up, according to a Reuters fact check published Friday. The verdict: the claim is missing context.

The AP called the race for Democrat Xavier Becerra at 8 p.m. Pacific on election night, as polls closed. Calling a race at poll close is standard practice when exit data and the underlying vote make the outcome clear, and by the most recent count Becerra led Republican Steve Hilton 64.6 percent to 35.4 percent with about 64 percent of the vote tallied — a margin no late count was going to erase.

The distinction matters because projection is not certification: news organizations project winners from data, while counties continue counting and certify results later. A fast call in a lopsided race is evidence of a lopsided race, not of a fixed one.

With two Senate races still uncalled and dozens of House races outstanding, expect more viral claims about the count in the days ahead — and more fact checks chasing them.

items.title: East Coast storm and flooding risk carry into the weekend
items.summary:
The cross-country storm system that has driven flooding rescues in the Southeast this week continues to push heavy rain toward the East Coast, keeping flood risk elevated into the weekend for communities already saturated.

Earlier in the week, catastrophic flooding on the Georgia–Tennessee border forced more than 100 rescues, and the same pattern — slow-moving rain over soaked ground — is what forecasters are watching as the system moves east. Urban and small-stream flooding are the main concerns where the heaviest bands set up.

For Ohio, the system arrives as the cold, damp pattern already in place: Solon tops out in the upper 40s Friday with temperatures falling through the day and showers likely by evening, before a sunnier, milder Sunday.

Residents in flood-prone areas along the storm's path are being urged to keep an eye on local alerts through Saturday, especially overnight, when flooding is hardest to see and most dangerous to drive into.

items.title: LeBron James plays in Cleveland tonight as a 76er for the first time — and the Cavs need the win
items.summary:
Rocket Arena hosts one of the season's most unusual homecomings on Friday night: LeBron James, in his first season with Philadelphia, plays in Cleveland as a Sixer for the first time. Tipoff is 7:30 p.m. on Prime Video, and the game doubles as the Cavaliers' first Emirates NBA Cup contest of the season.

The matchup matters in the standings, too. Philadelphia arrives at 8-1, riding five straight wins and sitting atop the East, with James averaging about 15.7 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 7.4 assists. Cleveland is 4-4 and has lost two straight to Oklahoma City, most recently 124-116 on Wednesday. The Sixers also won the first meeting on October 22, when the Cavs blew a 29-point lead and lost 114-106 in Philadelphia.

Injuries shape the night: Jarrett Allen is questionable after leaving Wednesday's game early with a right knee contusion, Tyrese Proctor and Peyton Watson are also questionable, and Jaylon Tyson and Nae'Qwan Tomlin are out. Former Cav Dean Wade, now a Sixer, predicted a madhouse — his word for every James return he witnessed from the home bench.

One sign of the times: for the first time in James's 13 years as a visiting player, the game did not sell out in advance, and the Cavs chose to hold their 2016 championship anniversary celebration on Saturday instead.

items.title: Judge sets a $1 million cash bond for the man charged in a Stow woman's killing
items.summary:
A judge has set a $1 million cash bond for Pierre Wade, 38, who was arraigned Friday in Stow Municipal Court on a murder charge in the death of Larretta Allison. The bond was confirmed by the court clerk following the arraignment.

Allison, 36, was found shot to death inside a home in the 4000 block of Vira Road on October 28, after officers were called around 5:30 p.m. to help a landlord with an eviction. She had suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to Stow police and the Summit County Medical Examiner's Office.

Wade was located in Cleveland by the Cuyahoga County Sheriff's Office and initially taken into custody on an unrelated failure-to-appear warrant. Stow police say a handgun was found in his vehicle.

The case now moves toward a grand jury. The bond level — cash only, at $1 million — signals the court views Wade as a significant flight or safety risk while the investigation continues.

items.title: Ohio measles cases are up nearly 600 percent this year, with 25 counties affected
items.summary:
Ohio has recorded 310 measles cases across 25 counties so far in 2026, according to the Ohio Department of Health dashboard updated November 5 — a rise of nearly 600 percent over last year. Cuyahoga County accounts for three of the cases.

There is a small piece of good news inside the numbers: the state added 14 new cases in the past week, a 61 percent drop from the 36 added the week before. Ashland County was the latest hotspot, reporting seven new cases to bring its yearly total to eight. The statewide count reflects earlier outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February, and the state's third outbreak of the year is still active.

Measles spreads with unusual ease and can be serious for infants and anyone immunocompromised — a relevant worry in a week when many Ohio families are visiting newborns and gathering indoors more as the weather turns.

Health officials' advice is unchanged: check vaccination records, and call ahead before visiting a doctor's office or urgent care with a suspected case so staff can prepare.

items.title: Acton and Brown did not just win Akron — they won every single precinct in the city
items.summary:
Governor-elect Amy Acton and Senator-elect Sherrod Brown completed a clean sweep of Akron on Tuesday, carrying all 120 of the city's precincts, according to a Signal Akron analysis of unofficial results. That includes flipping neighborhoods that had voted Republican.

The margins were emphatic. Acton took 74.7 percent of Akron's vote to Vivek Ramaswamy's 22.2 percent, and Brown won 72.1 percent to Jon Husted's 22.3 percent. All 12 Akron precincts that backed Donald Trump for president in 2024 voted for Acton this year, and 18 precincts gave both Democrats at least 85 percent.

Akron is a Democratic city, so the direction is not a surprise — the completeness of it is. A sweep with no precinct-level resistance at all points to how thoroughly the Republican ticket collapsed in Ohio's urban cores on Tuesday.

Results remain unofficial until counties certify, but margins of this size are not changing. The more useful question for both parties is whether the pattern repeats in Ohio's smaller cities in future cycles.

items.title: Northeast Ohio voters backed the big Cuyahoga levies — and flipped a congressional seat
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County voters approved both of the county's major levies on Tuesday, passing Issue 10 for developmental disabilities services with nearly 63 percent and Issue 11 for health and human services with about 60 percent, according to unofficial results. Together the measures add about $166.50 a year per $100,000 of property value.

Voters also approved charter Issues 12, 13, and 14, which limit some county executive powers. In congressional races, Democrat Brian Poindexter unseated Republican Representative Max Miller in the 7th District with 53 percent, and on County Council, Democrat Courtney Scheff's win over Mike Gallagher in District 5 leaves the council with no Republican members.

All of it sits inside the statewide story: Democrats flipped the governor's office and a U.S. Senate seat in Ohio on the same night, part of the national wave.

Nothing is final until certification — Cuyahoga County's is scheduled for November 24 — but none of these margins are within recount territory.

items.title: Downtown Cleveland's Huntington Building auction is pushed back a week, to November 10
items.summary:
The foreclosure auction of 925 Euclid Avenue — the former Huntington Building and downtown Cleveland's second-largest building by floor area — has been postponed by a week at the request of the court-appointed receiver. The auction is now set for November 10.

Judge Charles Fleming granted the delay so the receiver can, in the receiver's words, maximize the value and recovery of the property. The deadline for qualified bids has been extended to midnight November 8, and the sale hearing has moved to the morning of November 16. The receiver, John Lane of Mentor-based Inglewood Associates, has overseen the property since January.

The foreclosure was brought by lender Deutsche Bank's New York branch against an affiliate of Cleveland-based Millennia Companies after loan defaults and unpaid Cuyahoga County taxes totaling $40.1 million, according to court records. A Millennia-led team has pursued a residential-heavy redevelopment of the tower.

The building has been one of downtown's biggest question marks for years. Next week's auction will show whether a buyer with a workable plan finally exists.

baby.tip: Day 5 tip — the paperwork one, while it's quiet: Benji needs to be added to the health plan, and newborn enrollment windows are usually short, so it's worth a call to the fund office to confirm the exact deadline and what they need (typically the birth certificate or hospital record). One short call now beats a scramble later — and ask his pediatrician's office what they need on file too.
baby.fact: At five days old, Benji already knows his favorite scent — newborns can recognize their mother's smell within days of birth and will turn toward it. His hearing is tuned the same way: the voices he's heard most, yours and Kelly's, are the ones that settle him fastest.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for Day 5: Benjamin means 'son of the right hand' in Hebrew — traditionally the favored spot. Tiny mission to match: one photo today of Benji in someone's right-arm cradle hold, Moose supervising from a polite distance.
